title: Estimating physical quantities
prior_knowledge_summary: Every physical quantity consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit.
A bare numerical result is incomplete as a measurement record.
Arithmetic, scientific notation and basic geometry are available from prior school mathematics.
new_learning: A reasonable estimate is an approximate value supported by a familiar benchmark and a scale comparison.
An estimate should name the physical quantity, keep an appropriate unit attached and survive a plausibility check.
Bracketing clearly impossible scales is a reliable way to choose a sensible estimate.
not_yet_taught: SI base quantities and SI base units
Applications belonging to later Physics topics

visual_planning.reason: Six distinct visuals show the opening contradiction, a repeatable estimation route, benchmark comparison, scale bracketing, false precision and a spatial volume estimate.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Could an eraser have a mass of 3 kg?
content: Two labels fall off two objects. One label says mass = 0.03 kg and the other says mass = 3 kg. The objects are a small eraser and a loaded school bag. Which label belongs to which object?
You can answer without a balance. You already know something about the size and feel of each object. That stored experience is the beginning of a physical estimate.

figure.purpose: Create a scale contradiction that makes reasoned estimation necessary
figure.brief: Draw an eraser and a loaded school bag on a white-paper teacher sketch. Place loose labels 0.03 kg and 3 kg between them with curved question arrows, but do not attach either label to an object.
figure.alt_text: An eraser and a loaded school bag must be matched to mass labels of 0.03 kg and 3 kg.

blocks.title: An estimate is a reasoned approximation
content: An estimate is not a random number. It is an approximate value chosen from physical experience, a familiar benchmark and a comparison of scales.

A useful estimate does not need to equal a later measurement exactly. It needs to be close enough to describe the right scale. For the loaded bag, 3 kg is believable. Values such as 0.003 kg or 300 kg are on the wrong scale.
Keep Lesson 1 in view. First name the physical quantity. Then report one approximate numerical magnitude with an appropriate unit. A bare number cannot be judged clearly.

blocks.title: Use a four-step estimation route
content: Step 1: identify the physical quantity and the unit requested. Step 2: choose a familiar benchmark with the same kind of quantity. Step 3: decide whether the target is smaller, similar or larger. Step 4: state the estimate and check whether it fits the real situation.
Suppose you estimate the height of a classroom door in metres. A student is a useful height benchmark. The door must be a little taller than most students, so about 2 m is sensible.
The route matters more than guessing an exact hidden value. It gives you a reason that another person can inspect.

figure.purpose: Make the complete estimation procedure easy to reuse
figure.brief: Create a four-box flow sequence labelled quantity and unit, benchmark, scale comparison, estimate and check. Add a small door-and-student sketch under the boxes. Use arrows and sparse coloured annotations.
figure.alt_text: A four-step route moves from choosing the quantity and unit to a benchmark, scale comparison, estimate and check.

blocks.title: Estimate a bag by comparing its load
content: A school bag contains three textbooks, a laptop and a water bottle. We want its mass in kilograms. A familiar 1 kg food packet gives a useful mass benchmark.
The bag feels like several such packets, not a small fraction of one and not hundreds of them. A sensible estimate is about 5 kg. The word about signals that this is approximate.
Independent check: one student can lift the bag easily, but can feel its weight. That fits several kilograms and rules out both 0.005 kg and 500 kg.

figure.purpose: Show how a familiar benchmark is scaled to a target object
figure.brief: Draw a balance-style comparison with one 1 kg packet on the left and a loaded school bag on the right. Add five loose benchmark marks beside the bag and a final card reading about 5 kg. Keep the drawing qualitative rather than instrument-like.
figure.alt_text: A loaded school bag is compared with several 1 kg packets to support an estimate of about 5 kg.

blocks.title: Bracket the scale before choosing a value
content: A second way to estimate is to test widely separated scales. For a classroom door height, compare 0.2 m, 2 m and 20 m.
A height of 0.2 m is shorter than a school ruler. A height of 20 m is like a tall building. A classroom door sits between those extremes and is close to 2 m.
This scale-bracketing method works when your memory of an exact benchmark is uncertain. You eliminate physically impossible scales before selecting the believable one.

figure.purpose: Make rejection of impossible scales visible
figure.brief: Draw three vertical comparison panels for 0.2 m, 2 m and 20 m beside the same student. Show 0.2 m as far too short, 2 m as door-sized and 20 m as building-sized. Mark the middle panel with a simple plausibility tick.
figure.alt_text: Door-height candidates of 0.2 m, 2 m and 20 m are compared, with 2 m matching the familiar scale.

blocks.title: More digits do not make a rough estimate better
content: It can feel more scientific to write many calculator digits. That feeling comes from exact calculations, where extra information may support extra detail. An estimate is different because its starting benchmark is rough.
If a bag is judged to be around 5 kg, writing 5.0000 kg pretends that the mass is known very precisely. The extra zeroes add confidence that the evidence did not provide.
State a simple value that matches the quality of the comparison. Then use a physical check, not decorative digits, to make the estimate stronger.

figure.purpose: Contrast honest approximation with false precision
figure.brief: Draw two notebook estimate cards for the same rough bag comparison. One says about 5 kg with a reason and a tick. The other says 5.0000 kg with unsupported digits fading into question marks. Do not introduce formal significant-figure rules.
figure.alt_text: A reasoned estimate of about 5 kg is contrasted with an unsupported value of 5.0000 kg.

blocks.title: Build a volume estimate from a familiar cube
content: Now estimate the volume of a large apple in cubic centimetres. Imagine a cube with sides of about 5 cm. Its volume is 5 x 5 x 5 = 125 cm³.
A large apple is rounded and extends a little beyond that cube in some directions, so a nearby estimate such as 150 cm³ is reasonable. We are not claiming that every apple has exactly this volume.
Independent check: 15 cm³ would be much smaller than the imagined 5 cm cube, while 15 000 cm³ would be large enough for many apples. The estimate of 150 cm³ survives the scale check.

figure.purpose: Teach spatial estimation by comparison with a simple geometric benchmark
figure.brief: Draw a translucent hand-sketched 5 cm by 5 cm by 5 cm cube beside a rounded apple. Show the multiplication 5 x 5 x 5 = 125 cm cubed in an annotation, then a loose arrow to about 150 cm cubed. Keep the apple schematic and the labels sparse.
figure.alt_text: A large apple is compared with a 5 cm cube of volume 125 cubic centimetres to support an estimate near 150 cubic centimetres.

blocks.title: A good estimate tells a short physical story
content: Name the quantity and unit, choose a familiar benchmark, compare the target with it, state a simple approximate magnitude and reject impossible scales.
Mass, length, time and volume estimates use the same reasoning even though their benchmarks differ. The final value should be reasonable, not falsely exact.
Do not classify SI base quantities, use SI prefixes or analyse later-topic equations yet. The next lesson will build unit knowledge on top of the physical sense developed here.

concepts_taught: a reasonable estimate is an approximate value supported by physical experience and a benchmark
scale bracketing rejects values that are physically too small or too large
an estimate should not claim more precision than its rough evidence supports
misconceptions_addressed: an estimate is a random guess
an estimate must equal the later measured value exactly
more written digits automatically make an estimate better
skills_students_can_now_use: choose a familiar benchmark for a stated physical quantity
compare a target as smaller than, similar to or larger than a benchmark
bracket and reject impossible physical scales
report a reasonable approximate magnitude with an appropriate unit
check an estimate against the physical situation
next_lesson_can_assume: every physical quantity consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit
reasonable estimates can be built from familiar benchmarks and scale comparisons
an approximate value should retain an appropriate unit
impossible scales and false precision should be rejected
next_lesson_must_not_assume: SI base quantities or SI base units
